articles.title: EU fines X $140 million over ‘deceptive’ blue checkmarks
articles.summary: Today’s announcement follows the EU launching a multifaceted investigation into X in December 2023 regarding compliance with the Digital Services Act (DSA).
articles.body: The European Union has served Elon Musk’s X with a €120 million (about $140 million) penalty for violating the bloc’s digital service rulebook, in part for the “deceptive design” of its blue checkmark. Today’s announcement marks the first time that a company has been fined under the landmark Digital Services Act (DSA) law for curbing “illegal and harmful activities” on online platforms, and follows the EU launching a multifaceted investigation into X in December 2023. In July 2024, the EU ruled that X was failing to comply with obligations around advertising transparency, data access for researchers, and “dark patterns” — deceptive interface features designed to trick users. X’s blue checkmark system was specifically called out for deceiving users by allowing anyone to pay to be “verified,” making it harder to determine the authenticity of X accounts. In today’s announcement, the European Commission noted that while the DSA doesn’t require user verification, “it clearly prohibits online platforms from falsely claiming that users have been verified.” “Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU,” the bloc’s tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement. “The DSA protects users. The DSA gives researchers the way to uncover potential threats. The DSA restores trust in the online environment. With the DSA’s first non-compliance decision, we are holding X responsible for undermining users’ rights and evading accountability.” The EU can charge companies up to 6 percent of their global revenue for DSA violations. As X is a private company — purchased by Musk for $44 billion in October 2022 and again by his artificial intelligence company, X AI, in March 2025 for $33 billion — it’s unclear what its potential maximum penalty could have been. X can appeal the fine, but now has 60 working days to inform the EU of the measures it will take to change the “deceptive” use of blue checkmarks, and 90 days for its planned fixes for the other violations. Failure to meet those deadlines could result in more penalty payments. European lawmakers had deliberated how large a fine to issue according to The New York Times, reporting that regulators sought to make an example of X as a warning to other companies while weighing the risks of sparking retaliation from President Donald Trump amid ongoing trade disputes. Musk, alongside the leadership of other US tech giants, has encouraged the president to stop the EU from taking advantage of US companies. The 2023 investigation was also launched to scrutinize X’s moderation practices and the dissemination of illegal or harmful content on the platform, which is currently still ongoing and could incur further penalties. The EU has criticized X over rising levels of disinformation following its acquisition by Musk. In January, EU lawmakers pledged to “energetically” push the X investigation forward over concerns with Musk’s promotion of Germany’s far-right party leader on the platform. Musk has used X to rally behind other far-right personalities and sparked outrage after pulling a controversial gesture during his speech at Trump’s inauguration.

articles.title: Trump Flexes Legal Muscle to Expand Power Over US Elections
articles.summary: The Justice Department’s aggressive strategy includes suing states for voter records, investigating election officials and fighting for GOP redistricting mea...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump is pursuing extraordinary legal tactics to assert greater federal control over US elections, testing the boundaries of Washington's power over how Americans vote as his Republican Party seeks to keep its majority in Congress this fall.

While the US Constitution largely puts states in charge of elections, Trump has sought to reach into virtually every corner of the voting process as he boosts baseless accusations of widespread fraud that critics warn is eroding public trust. The president has empowered the nation's top law enforcement agency, the Justice Department, to pressure states to align with the administration's agenda — including threatening to prosecute local officials — and pursue Republican redistricting goals in court.

The result is a collision between executive power and the states' traditional authority, with the courts increasingly becoming the battleground. A prime example is Trump's push to curb mail-in voting, which is used by tens of millions of Americans including the president. The Justice Department repeatedly turned to the Supreme Court to intervene as lower courts blocked the administration from rushing to implement new mail-in ballot restrictions at Trump's direction in the Nov. 3 midterms.

Even after the Supreme Court last week rebuffed the administration's push to quickly implement new Postal Service restrictions on mail-in ballots, Attorney General Todd Blanche said they will comply, but vowed to press ahead on the broader strategy, telling reporters that the loss "doesn't mean that we're not going to do everything in this administration that we can to make sure that there are free and fair elections."

Enforcing US laws in elections has historically been part of the department's mission, but more often focused on addressing racial discrimination, language and disability access at polls and other barriers to voting. Critics and boosters agree the agency under Trump has been more aggressive than recent past administrations — though they diverge on whether that's good or bad.

Some are ringing alarm bells as Republicans defend their tight majorities in Congress in November and begin to lay the groundwork for the 2028 presidential contest. This week, a federal judge in Washington refused to let the Justice Department delay responding to a Democratic National Committee lawsuit seeking any internal records about plans for ballot seizures, after the party organization argued there was a "very real threat" of such a move in the midterms.

articles.title: Homens são flagrados em porta-malas aberto em cima da Terceira Ponte | G1
articles.standfirst: Vídeo mostra o carro circulando ao lado de outros veículos a quase 70 metros de altura entre Vila Velha e Vitória.
articles.summary: Vídeo mostra o carro circulando ao lado de outros veículos a quase 70 metros de altura entre Vila Velha e Vitória.
articles.body:
Uma cena chamou a atenção de quem passava pela Terceira Ponte, que liga Vila Velha a Vitória, no Espírito Santo, nesta semana. Um carro foi flagrado trafegando com dois homens sentados na ponta do porta-malas aberto, com as pernas para fora do veículo.

Um terceiro homem também aparece no vídeo com o corpo para fora da janela traseira do lado direito do veículo. O vídeo circulou nas redes sociais (assista acima).

As imagens mostram ainda que os três carregavam câmeras e aparentavam fazer registros de um grupo de motociclistas que trafegava pela ponte. O carro permaneceu com o pisca-alerta ligado durante o trecho registrado. O vídeo não informa a data em que a gravação foi feita.

Questionada sobre o caso, a Polícia Militar do Espírito Santo informou que não recebeu acionamento relacionado à situação, mas afirmou que as imagens mostram possíveis infrações de trânsito.

Segundo o especialista de trânsito, capitão Anthony Moraes Costa, o artigo 235 do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB) estabelece que conduzir pessoas nas partes externas do veículo, salvo em casos autorizados, é uma infração grave , com aplicação de multa de R$ 195,23 e retenção do veículo para transbordo.

Homens são flagrados em porta-malas aberto e com o corpo para fora de janela de carro na Terceira Ponte, no Espírito Santo — Foto: Reprodução

Já o artigo 169 do CTB prevê como infração leve dirigir sem atenção ou sem os cuidados indispensáveis à segurança. Com multa de R$ 88,38 e acréscimo de três pontos na Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH).

A Companhia Estadual de Transportes Coletivos de Passageiros do Estado do Espírito Santo (Ceturb-ES) informou que não recebeu, até a publicação desta reportagem, reclamações ou registros relacionados ao caso mostrado no vídeo.

Segundo a companhia, as imagens do caso foram separadas pela companhia e estão à disposição da autoridade de trânsito. Já a apuração da forma como os veículos são conduzidos e uma eventual responsabilização cabem às autoridades competentes.

*Texto produzido por Emanoele Gobbi, aluna do 29º Curso de Residência em Jornalismo. Este conteúdo teve orientação e edição de Vitor Ferri.

articles.title: China now makes up a record 40% of all global container exports—and it’s a sign Trump’s tariffs meant to punish Chinese firms have fallen flat
articles.summary: “The tariff policies of the last two years have been an unmitigated disaster. They have made exactly what we're talking about worse for the United States.”
articles.body:
China keeps growing its share of global cargo sales, indicating the Trump administration's tariffs meant to punish the country are instead an obstacle that China has successfully navigated.

China now accounts for 40% of the world's container exports on a rolling three-month basis, a 2.5% increase from nine months ago and its highest-ever levels, Jens Eskelund, president of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, told the Financial Times on Tuesday.

For Europe, China's swelling share of global shipments represents a growing trade imbalance between the continents, Eskelund warned. As more cheaper goods from China flood European markets, European manufacturers are squeezed out, and the continent loses out on global market share for exports and China sells its goods for cheap elsewhere.

The U.S. is facing a similar fate, harkening back to the "China Shock" of the early 2000s, representing a surge of Chinese products on American shelves following its entry into the World Trade Organization, throttling U.S. manufacturing and leaving pockets of America with massive job losses and stagnant wages. Economists predict the impending "China Shock 2.0" will extend beyond retail shelves to technology like AI infrastructure and electric vehicles.

"China really is becoming the workshop of the world," Jeremi Suri, a public affairs and history professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told Fortune . "And what that means is that almost every global economy is one way or another dependent on China."

What's troubling to economists and policy experts is how the U.S. got here. While China's path to becoming a global export behemoth has been decades in the making, President Donald Trump's trade philosophy of inundating China with import taxes may be, in large part, to blame for this more recent shift.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will meet for a two-day summit beginning on Wednesday.

"The tariff policies of the last two years have been an unmitigated disaster," Suri said. "They have made exactly what we're talking about worse for the United States."

How did tariffs pave the way for China's growing container export share?

Part of China's rise to power in trades comes from a natural cycle. The U.S. began transitioning from a manufacturing economy to a service economy in the 1950s—and by the 1970s, China had meanwhile ended its isolationist policies like high tariffs and cemented its role in global trade when it joined the WTO 25 years ago. Buoyed by an undervalued currency , Chinese firms can charge up to 30% less than other countries to export goods, leading to a glut of production to be sold overseas.

images.caption: Economists say China has adapted to President Donald Trump's tariffs. · Fortune · Evan Vucci/POOL/AFP—Getty Images

articles.title: Trump and Xi Buy Time on Trade With Neither Able to Afford a Fight
articles.summary: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping agreed to maintain a trade truce until early 2027, with neither ready to upend relations between the world’s biggest economies ev...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Donald Trump and Xi Jinping agreed to maintain a trade truce until early 2027, with neither ready to upend relations between the world's biggest economies even as tensions persist over rare earths, technology curbs and Taiwan.

Just as Xi landed in the US on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that an agreement struck by the leaders last year will now run an additional two months until Jan. 10. That removes much of the tension around Xi's first state visit to the US since 2015, and clears the way for two more meetings between the presidents planned in the coming months at summits in Shenzhen and Miami.

Still, the brief extension shows that the "constructive strategic stability" underpinning the relationship remains fragile. The US has accused China of failing to live up to pledges to provide a steady flow of rare earths, while Beijing remains confident that its grip over the elements crucial to defense and high-tech manufacturing will deter Trump from reimposing sky-high tariffs.

"We can live with that because we are confident that within two months the US cannot become independent of Chinese rare-earth supply," said Wu Xinbo, director of Fudan University's Center for American Studies and a former adviser to China's Foreign Ministry. "They'll come back and beg for Chinese exports of rare earth magnets to the US."

News of the extension appeared to reduce the immediate risk of a supply disruption, hurting shares of companies seeking to provide alternatives to Chinese rare earth supplies. Toyo Engineering Corp. slid about 9% in Tokyo and Australia's Lynas Rare Earths Ltd. fell as much as 5%. The broader markets showed little enthusiasm, with China's benchmark CSI 300 Index falling 1.7% and MSCI's gauge of Asian stocks dropping 0.8%, also pressured by elevated oil prices and US bond yields.

Bessent on Wednesday met with his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng in Washington to hammer out the terms, building from talks held in New York last weekend. Even so, the US treasury secretary made his displeasure clear while announcing the truce.

"There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side," Bessent told Fox News. US officials had spelled out their expectations and now wanted to see if Beijing "could be a bit more fulsome in enacting the agreement" in the coming months.

articles.title: Warren Buffett’s final words of warning as Berkshire chairman: US dollar ‘going to hell.’ Shockproof your nest egg now
articles.summary: “Fiscal policy is what scares me in the United States.”
articles.body:

Warren Buffett spent more than 60 years building Berkshire Hathaway into one of America's most powerful companies. Now, at 96, he has relinquished the chairman's seat — and a warning he delivered at his final shareholder meeting as CEO sounds especially striking in light of that farewell.

"We wouldn't want to be owning anything that we thought was in a currency that was really going to hell, and that's the big thing we worry about with the United States currency," Buffett told shareholders (1) in May 2025.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

A record 45% of central banks plan to grow gold reserves — and many investors are following suit. Get your free gold IRA guide from Priority Gold

Buffett wasn't declaring that the dollar had already collapsed. He was warning about what relentless government spending and borrowing could eventually do to its value.

"Fiscal policy is what scares me in the United States," he said.

The federal government has spent more than it collects for decades, covering the shortfall by borrowing and piling ever more debt onto its balance sheet. Buffett warned that this cannot continue indefinitely without consequences.

"We're operating at a fiscal deficit now that is unsustainable over a very long period of time," he said. "We are doing something that is unsustainable, and it has the aspect to it that it gets uncontrollable to a certain point."

Since then, the arithmetic has only become more alarming. Through the first 11 months of fiscal 2026, the federal government ran up another $1.97 trillion (2) deficit. Meanwhile, the national debt has surged past a staggering $40 trillion (3).

That number is almost too large to comprehend. But beneath America's sprawling fiscal problem lies something that affects every household: the value of its money.

Buffett acknowledged that governments "can issue paper money," but warned that "the natural course of government is to make the currency worth less over time, and that's got important consequences."

Americans don't have to look far to see those consequences, as inflation has steadily eroded the dollar's purchasing power for decades. According to the inflation calculator put out by the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (4), $100 in 2026 has the same purchasing power as just $11.61 did in 1970.

articles.title: Trump on AI talks with Xi: ‘I want to leave it exactly where it is’
articles.summary: President Trump said Thursday that he wants to leave AI “exactly where it is” ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. “A big day with President Xi of China,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is.…
articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday that he wants to leave AI “exactly where it is” ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“A big day with President Xi of China,” he wrote on Truth Social . “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!”

Trump, who is pushing to rebrand AI as “ super intelligence ,” has repeatedly argued against establishing new guardrails in recent weeks despite dire warnings from researchers about the technology’s risks to humanity.

In a speech before the United Nations on Tuesday, he suggested the U.S. “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” on AI.

This stands in sharp contrast to remarks from top AI leaders. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei both appeared before the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday and urged global cooperation on AI safeguards.

“In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don’t always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and the collective good in the face of a powerful new technology,” Altman said. “We believe this must be one of those times.”

Trump is set to meet with Xi in Washington later Thursday morning. It is the Chinese leader’s first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.

AI is expected to be a key issue on the agenda , although the prospect of a breakthrough appears relatively low as the two superpowers race one another to develop the technology.

articles.title: The vibes are bad for Flock in Washington
articles.summary: A Senate Judiciary subcommittee scrutinized Flock’s surveillance network at a hearing that its CEO declined to attend, according to Chair Josh Hawley (R-MO).
articles.body: Flock is in the hot seat in Washington, even if its CEO declined to actually face senators at a hearing about its “AI Surveillance Network” on Wednesday. “There’s many players in this industry, but there’s one name that really stands out above the rest, and that is Flock,” Senate Judiciary crime and counterterrorism subcommittee chair Josh Hawley (R-MO) said. “If you haven’t heard of Flock, all I have to say is, Flock’s probably heard of you.” Though the CEOs of Flock and peer companies Axon, Motorola Solutions, and Verkada declined to testify, according to Hawley, seats in the hearing room were in high demand. A standby line stretched down the hallway even after they were filled. Instead of the CEOs, the hearing featured testimony from cybersecurity and legal experts, a sheriff whose department ended its Flock contract after allegedly receiving slippery answers about its AI use, and a Florida woman who said she spent 13 days in jail after her car was incorrectly identified by Flock cameras as being connected to a crime scene. Verkada spokesperson Virginia Ramsey said the company provided information to the subcommittee to assist in preparation even though its CEO could not attend. “As we’ve explained to the Subcommittee, none of our customers can search a national Verkada network – because none exists. Our customers can only access the data in their own systems,” Ramsey said. Representatives for the other companies invited did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. The federal hearing shows just how much the conversation around Flock has escalated, from concerns within individual police departments about reported abuse by cops, to raucous city council meetings and testy state capitol hearings — and now, a Congressional hearing. Less than two months before Election Day for the midterms, lawmakers across the aisle appeared largely aligned and even chummy over their unease about automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that hoover up location data for Americans who haven’t been accused of crimes, and can store that information, in many cases, for an entire month. Lawmakers expressed concern about how securely Flock is able to store its vast trove of images, which cybersecurity engineer Benn Jordan said he was able to access with minimal technical maneuvering, in an incident Flock has said it’s since addressed. Jordan said he’s more recently been granted greater access to Flock to evaluate it, and said its security has improved from a year ago, but broader industry-wide issues persist. The lawmakers also took issue with how easy it appears to be for officers to access Flock data, and said it’s distinct from traditional license plate readers, whose systems don’t construct the same dossier of connected information on individual vehicles. Democrats like Sens. Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) asked how federal immigration authorities could be legally barred from accessing Flock data, and about potential loopholes, which one witness said could be as simple as getting a sympathetic local officer to perform a search on the agency’s behalf. Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) asked whether officers in states that restrict abortion access could track people seeking reproductive care across state lines. On the Republican side, Hawley pointed out that similar concerns could apply for gun owners. “For those of us who are supporters of the Second Amendment, we’ve long feared national databases of any kind. You could easily put these cameras up in front of a gun show or near a gun store or a range. You can put them up in front of pregnancy care centers, and you can do all the same things that Senator Booker was talking about,” Hawley said. But it’s still early days for legislating around Flock and other ALPRs. After the hearing, Hawley told reporters that he hadn’t heard of the company until a month or two ago, and “we’re all just getting up to speed on this.” He said he’d still like to hear from the CEOs directly, but subpoenaing them to appear would require a full committee vote, and he hadn’t yet discussed that with Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (R-IA). Then there’s the issue of whether President Donald Trump, who recently said “I like them” of the cameras, would support legislation that restrains them. Hawley said he hasn’t asked that yet. “In Missouri, we’ve been using license plate readers forever… but that’s really different than the technology we’re talking about today,” Hawley told reporters. “I think that’s something that I’ve only recently come to appreciate, and I bet most folks are just getting up to speed on. Citizens know though. They know when they’re being tracked. They don’t want to be tracked and treated like criminals. And I think law-abiding citizens just should not be treated like criminals.”

articles.title: FAA blames error messages for switch to backup fiber line before outage
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) blamed error messages that caused the agency to switch to a backup fiber line that halted flights in multiple northeast airports this week. The FAA said it was advised on Sunday by L3Harris, a technology contractor, to switch to the backup lines in order to begin troubleshooting at a Philadelphia…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) blamed error messages that caused the agency to switch to a backup fiber line that halted flights in multiple northeast airports this week.

The FAA said it was advised on Sunday by L3Harris, a technology contractor, to switch to the backup lines in order to begin troubleshooting at a Philadelphia air traffic control facility, according to Reuters . The agency continued that a New Jersey Transit contractor on Monday accidentally cut the backup fiber ⁠line.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said during a Wednesday conference that, “We need to get rid of the old system,” per Reuters.

“When it fails, ​we just don’t have ​the redundancy that we ⁠would get if we had a modern architecture,” he stated.

The outage affected flights at major airports including Newark Liberty International Airport and John F. Kennedy International Airport ahead of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City. At Newark, roughly 1 in 3 departing flights were canceled Monday, according to data from FlightAware .

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law last year, provided the FAA with $12.5 billion to modernize the national air traffic control system. Officials from the aviation agency have asked for an additional $10 billion from Congress to upgrade the air traffic control system.

Bedford also said during a press conference Monday that the 600-foot fiber cable cut was somewhere between Newark and New Brunswick, N.J. The FAA administrator later said the fiber cable was cut earlier Monday.

He confirmed that about 90 flights had been diverted as a result of the outage, and the FAA does not know the number of cancellations.

“This is why we’re asking for a budget to replace all of this stuff,” he added.

When asked about the outages, the FAA referred to a social media post from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, writing, “This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future.”

An L3Harris spokesperson told The Hill, “L3Harris is fully committed to the safety and reliability of the National Airspace System. We work closely with the FAA each day to support the safety-critical systems they rely on, and we followed established protocols throughout this event, as we do with all events. For more information about this specific event, we’d refer you to the FAA.”

articles.title: Phone weather forecast often wrong? Here’s why
articles.summary: When the weekend actually rolls around, the highs, lows and chance of rain numbers you were seeing on your phone app may be totally different. It could easily rain when it says it wouldn’t, or be way hotter than expected.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – With a busy weekend ahead — and a Nor’easter, tropical storms or even a chance of snow threatening to disrupt your weekend plans, depending on where you live — you may be refreshing the weather forecast on your phone every few hours.

But when the weekend actually rolls around, the highs, lows and chances of rain you see on your phone app may be totally different. It could easily rain when it says it wouldn’t, or be way hotter than expected.

Smart phone weather apps can be wrong for two main reasons, Nexstar senior meteorologist Jim Danner explained.

First, an app is only as good as the data that’s feeding it. Often, what models are being used to populate those forecasts isn’t transparent to the average person, and the quality can vary widely from app to app.

“Everybody wants to do a weather app now,” Danner said. “So if everybody’s doing it differently you’re going to get different numbers.”

The other problem, Danner explained, has to do with the uncertainty of predicting weather more than a few days out.

“When you start getting to seven days and beyond, you’re really pushing the envelope there,” he said. Danner, who has an iPhone, said in his experience that the standard Apple Weather app does pretty well predicting weather three to five days out, but tends to be less accurate further than that (as any forecast tends to be).

If you want a better shot at getting the right forecast, Danner suggested checking the National Weather Service or the forecast from your local TV meteorologist. Meteorologists that live and work in a market know which weather models are most accurate for that region’s seasonal patterns, topography and quirks.

“When a forecaster comes on duty, their first order of business is to become familiar with what is currently happening in the weather. This includes looking at satellite imagery, surface data, precipitation reports, and getting a briefing from other forecasters on duty,” explained meteorologist Mark Bloomer in a post for the National Weather Service .

They combine data with their knowledge of the atmosphere to make predictions about what will happen later that day, tomorrow and beyond.

“Forecasters deal with many forecast models that are run several times a day and must decide which ones to rely on based on how well they seem to be handling current weather, how realistic their output is, and how consistent the forecast models are being from one run to the next,” Bloomer continued. “The forecaster may even decide that no model can be relied on at that time.”

“I would spend well over an hour putting together my forecast every morning,” Danner said, remembering when he worked as a local meteorologist in Texas. “These meteorologists make a living knowing their region. … So you get that human touch.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang talks about AI and climate change like a supervillain
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang talked about AI inflicting “an enormous amount of pain and suffering” through its energy use.
articles.body: As Jensen Huang puts it, AI can help fight climate change — but only if it inflicts “an enormous amount of pain and suffering” first. The Nvidia CEO discussed the future of energy and AI’s impact on our planet in the latest episode of The Ezra Klein Show. But his comments boil down to the same accelerationist spin we’ve seen from a variety of tech leaders as well as President Donald Trump. They promise that AI will be such a gift to humanity that it’s worth the damage caused by data centers currently running on dirty energy. Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring in the interview. He’s right that there will be pain. People are already suffering from fires and floods exacerbated by climate change. People are already dying earlier because of air pollution from fossil fuels. But Huang, with a net worth of around $192.6 billion, will not pay the price of the pollution his company creates through energy-hungry chip factories and data centers. Huang tells Klein, after complaining that the US hasn’t built out enough fossil fuel plants, that: > It’s kind of like, in order to save you, they’ve got to hurt you first — that’s the nature of surgery. They’ve got to cut you open to save you. They’ve got to inflict an enormous amount of pain and suffering on you so that they can save you. And so I think AI’s kind of like that. That’s the bit that gives Thanos energy. Resources are too limited and so after disappearing half of humanity, the Marvel supervillain believes, things will be much rosier. (“I will shred this universe down to its last atom, and then create a new one, teeming with life that knows not what it has lost but only what it has been given,” he tells the Avengers.) Huang goes on to say: > Over the next several years we have to unfortunately use fossil fuels, because we just don’t have enough sustainable energy to make a difference. And then after that, hopefully, we can transition to that. For context, nearly every country on Earth agreed to limit climate change when they adopted the Paris agreement in 2015. The accord sets a goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030 and reaching net zero around 2050. That can only happen with swift transition to carbon-free energy like renewables and nuclear. Here’s just a short list of terrible things getting worse when we stall that progress to pursue advances in AI: * Earth is expected to lose 99 percent of its coral reefs. Those reefs support coastal economies, and also serve as a buffer protecting communities from tropical storms, flooding, and coastal erosion. * One in 10 people around the world, 770 million people, already face “acute risk” from sea level rise. * Since 2001, peak daily wildfire growth rates have more than doubled in the western US. Wildfires are faster, more frequent, and more intense. These effects are showing up in Huang’s backyard, even if he’s insulated from them. He mentions in the interview that he doesn’t know what his own address is. However, he reportedly bought a $7.5 million home on Maui in 2004 — before wildfires devastated the island in 2023. That year, an Nvidia spokesperson confirmed with The Verge that the Huangs “have owned the same home in Maui for many years.” Huang’s property reportedly escaped damage, and the Nvidia spokesperson told me that the Huangs “donated significantly to local relief efforts.” But despite the philanthropy from tech billionaires with residences on Maui, the inferno also inflamed tensions over luxury properties’ hold on Maui’s water supply. “Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community,” Maui County Councilmember Keani Rawlins-Fernandez told me at the time. “It underscores the stark disparity between Indigenous people who want to mālama ‘āina, care for our land, and those who see Hawaii as a vacation destination.” While greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels makes wildfires more dangerous by exacerbating hot, dry conditions, climate change isn’t entirely to blame for the flames that razed much of Lahaina on Maui. I reported at the time that previous generations of wealthy land grabbers primed the islands to burn. The US annexed the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1898, egged on by American plantation owners who wanted to evade import taxes. They cleared native vegetation for their businesses, allowing invasive grasses to take hold and make the landscape much more flammable than it used to be. So when I hear Huang make the case now that there will need to be sacrifices in the name of AI progress, it reminds me that we’ve seen this playbook before. An industry that wants to grow at any cost. And nearby communities and their descendants are just supposed to live with the aftermath. Huang mentions growing community opposition to data centers in the interview with Klein, and scolds other companies for not spreading the good news with residents about how efficient data centers purportedly are before they start construction. “If they don’t want data centers to be built in their town or whatever it is, then so be it. But if you’re going to build in their town, be sure to go there and let them know what’s coming,” he says. “I am inevitable,” Thanos notoriously said — and apparently, so are AI data centers. Even so, data centers don’t actually have to be as polluting as they are turning out to be. In the interview, Huang also (unfairly) attributes record renewable energy purchases to AI. He blames climate action for stalling the construction of energy infrastructure, presumably for fossil fuels. > I think we just have to acknowledge that we got ourselves really gummed up in climate change and sustainable energy, and as a result, we just didn’t plan enough energy production. Then he proclaims that AI is “the best opportunity we have” to “turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable.” He sees AI accelerating demand for clean energy in the long term. But AI already needs a lot of energy now, and fossil fuels are what we’ve got. But renewables were already the fastest-growing sources of new electricity generation before the recent generative AI boom. It’s generally cheaper to generate power from a wind or solar farm than a new gas or coal plant. But Trump, who lined his campaign coffers with money from the fossil fuel industry, is incentivizing the development of gas and coal plants to power data centers. And now, data centers are in turn spurring the development of far more fossil fuel infrastructure. Air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028, according to a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology. Nevertheless, “A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, a senior director of the Environmental Protection Network, a group made up of EPA alumni, said in a recent press briefing on the growing health risks posed by data centers. It also depends on the attitudes of industry leaders like Huang. If other people’s pain and suffering is the price you’re willing to pay for so-called progress, that says less about what’s possible and more about your own personal priorities.

articles.title: 75 percent fearful, concerned about AI: Poll
articles.summary: A majority of Americans are worried about AI’s progress as tech industry leaders and lawmakers call for its development to slow, according to a poll released Thursday. Three quarters of respondents to CNN’s new survey reported some level of “fear and concern” when it came to “growth and development of AI technology.” The remaining 25…
articles.body:
A majority of Americans are worried about AI’s progress as tech industry leaders and lawmakers call for its development to slow, according to a poll released Thursday.

Three quarters of respondents to CNN’s new survey reported some level of “fear and concern” when it came to “growth and development of AI technology.” The remaining 25 percent of those polled instead said they felt “hope and excitement” surrounding its development.

Out of poll participants who evaluated AI’s growth positively, 7 percent felt “strongly” on the topic, while 18 percent were “somewhat” enthusiastic. In contrast, 43 percent of those fearful of the emerging technology had strong opinions on it.

The poll comes amid broader political discussion around the limits of AI regulation, as concerns mount surrounding its environmental and data privacy implications. While Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) float legislation seeking to ban artificial “superintelligence,” President Trump and his allies have embraced the technology.

Over the weekend, Trump announced plans for the creation of an “AI Force” and the appointment of a “czar” to oversee the technology’s development, though he has rejected calls for federal regulations.

Trump, in a Truth Social post, referred to concerns about a lack of federal AI guardrails as a “hoax,” saying he would not make space for the technology’s “decimation” as its U.S.-based industry leaders compete with other countries.

“AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP [gross domestic product]. We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” he wrote on Saturday.

In the CNN poll, 71 percent said the federal government wasn’t putting enough effort into AI regulation, while 10 percent said lawmakers were doing too much to address the topic. Eighteen percent described their AI regulation efforts as sufficient.

The CNN poll took place from Sept. 16-17, featuring 1,206 respondents and a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percent.

The Senate Finance Committee voted 15-12, with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) joining all Republicans. Klomp is already a powerful senior adviser…
articles.body:
A key Senate committee Thursday advanced the nomination of Chris Klomp to be deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), setting him up for a later floor vote for confirmation.

The Senate Finance Committee voted 15-12, with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) joining all Republicans.

Klomp is already a powerful senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has led negotiations over “ most favored nation ” drug pricing deals between the Trump administration and pharmaceutical companies, and he has been actively involved in high-profile hiring decisions.

“Part of my responsibility is to enable the smooth operations of the department. I’m responsible for personnel, among other things,” Klomp said last week during his confirmation hearings across both the Finance Committee and Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. “My job is to make sure that we have everything.”

During his hearings, Klomp was questioned about vaccines and how he would respond to Trump and Kennedy’s often untrue statements on the subject.

“I want somebody who’s going to stand up to the lies,” Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said.

Wyden on Thursday said Kennedy lied when he pledged he would not do anything to restrict access to vaccines or discourage people from taking them. Wyden said Klomp was “complicit” in those lies.

Wyden also pressed Klomp to disclose details about the drug pricing agreements he helped negotiate.

The deals are expected to exempt drugs from certain Medicare price deductions, as well as to protect the companies from tariffs. In exchange, the companies agreed to sell certain drugs to Medicaid at the same price as peer countries. But the details have remained secret.

“All I have received are excuses and misrepresentations,” Wyden said.

articles.title: White House seeks to pressure Democrats to move faster on permitting reform deal
articles.summary: As a key Democratic negotiator says a deal to speed up infrastructure projects could be months away, the Trump administration is saying it may not be willing to wait that long. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) told reporters Thursday that a permitting reform deal could pass in the lame duck, but the White House is indicating…
articles.body:
As a key Democratic negotiator says a deal to speed up infrastructure projects could be months away, the Trump administration is saying it may not be willing to wait that long.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) told reporters Thursday that a permitting reform deal could pass in the lame duck, but the White House is indicating that the concessions it is offering Democrats could expire by that point.

“The Administration and congressional Republicans agreed to a strong bipartisan offer. The Democrats have since refused to take yes for an answer. If they think that the administration is going to freeze these concessions until the lame duck, they are severely mistaken,” a White House official said via email.

The administration’s message comes ahead of the heavily watched midterm elections, where Republicans are expected to lose seats as high fuel prices hamper the economy and an increasing number of Americans are expressing disapproval of President Trump.

Getting an infrastructure deal done by that point could be a significant win for the administration to point to as it makes its case that voters should support the GOP.

Whitehouse, meanwhile, described the wait until after the midterms as necessary to give lawmakers enough time to digest the agreement and adequately campaign ahead of the November contest.

“I think there is consensus that the House is not likely to come back before the election, and that the time that is necessary for these ordinary Senate procedures to take place is a bit inconsistent with the rush by Republican senators to get the hell out of here and home campaigning, so I think that is moving us towards votes after the election as the best avenue for passage of this bill,” he told reporters.

A Senate Democratic aide told The Hill that the vote’s timing was an agreement between Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

For years, Democrats and Republicans have been trying to come to an agreement to speed up the buildout of infrastructure, particularly energy projects, a process that has become known as permitting reform.

Democrats have pushed for bolstering renewable power and the electric grid, while Republicans have pushed for fossil fuels and cuts across the board to environmental reviews and legal challenges.

Disagreements have been exacerbated in recent years by the Trump administration’s efforts to block or otherwise hamper renewable energy projects.

Whitehouse told reporters that the White House has indicated better treatment for solar and wind could come with the deal.

“There has been a general agreement that with this bill will come improvements in the treatment of wind and solar,” he said.

“Some assurances have been fairly specific; others still need to be clarified. I appreciate very much what the Trump administration has done to move in this direction, but in order to brief colleagues on what this really means, we need just a bit more clarity on exactly what return to regular order for wind and solar projects looks like,” he added.

Whitehouse indicated, however, that a deal was in reach.

“We are over the hump on the deal-breaker issues, so we’re in a very good place on the substance of the bill,” he said, adding that text could be finalized in “days, maybe even hours,” which could kick off the process of allowing senators to consider the bill and suggest changes.

articles.title: CDC adds 1 measles death to US tracker, while Pennsylvania reports disease killed 4
articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added one measles death to its online database, marking the first fatal case the agency has acknowledged tied to the country’s 2026 outbreak. While CDC’s website does not list when and where the death occurred, the update follows weeks of criticism from Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D)…
articles.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added one measles death to its online database , marking the first fatal case the agency has acknowledged tied to the country’s 2026 outbreak.

While CDC’s website does not list when and where the death occurred, the update follows weeks of criticism from Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) over the omission of his state’s four reported measles-related deaths from the agency’s tracker.

Pennsylvania first reported two infant deaths tied to the illness in late August and added two more in mid-September, while the CDC’s update came Wednesday, The Washington Post reported . These fatal cases come amid a record-setting year for measles in the country, with the number of reported infections reaching a 35-year high.

The past exclusion of Pennsylvania’s measles-related deaths from the CDC’s platform sparked a public feud between Shapiro and Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The Democratic governor said last week that Kennedy “doesn’t believe that measles is an issue,” accusing the HHS leader of not being “grounded in reality.”

A footnote on the CDC measles dashboard states the public health agency is “aware” of other “probable measles cases” but that the website only includes confirmed cases. The agency has historically relied on state health departments to confirm cases within their jurisdictions.

HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison said in a statement to The Hill that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) verified and notified the CDC of the new measles-related death, though she did not say when the notification occurred.

“Through its standard process, NCHS verified that the death occurred and that measles was listed as the underlying cause of death,” Jamison said. “This is now reflected on the CDC website.”

Jamison added that the CDC is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists “to develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles” to create “consistent classification and reporting” of these deaths.

Earlier this month, Kennedy acknowledged that measles caused the death of an infant in Pennsylvania after a Lancaster County coroner confirmed a cause of death. He accused Shapiro of having “politicized” deaths tied to measles in the commonwealth.

The CDC has reported 3,471 measles infections across the nation, including 745 in Pennsylvania, as of Sept. 17. Pennsylvania’s health department reported 835 cases this year, including 111 in the past week, according to a Wednesday update.

articles.title: Trump Advisers Analyzing Impact of Short-Term Diesel Export Ban
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s economic advisers are analyzing the ramifications of a potential short-term ban on US diesel exports, underscoring the seriousness o...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's economic advisers are analyzing the ramifications of a potential short-term ban on US diesel exports, underscoring the seriousness of the administration's consideration of the idea.

Senator John Hoeven, a Republican from North Dakota, said the study being conducted by National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer aims to inform the administration's decision-making on possible export curbs.

"The idea is that you get Bessent and Greer and Hassett to do that analysis and if, on a short-term basis — and we are in harvest season right now — it would show that it would help, then it is something we should consider doing," Hoeven said.

Several farm-state lawmakers have urged Trump to limit foreign sales of US diesel, as conflicts in Russia and the Middle East take supplies offline and spike prices for the fuel right at the peak of the fall harvest season in the US.

Diesel is essential for powering farm equipment and is a critical fuel for modern shipping, propelling freight trains, long-haul trucks and delivery vans. And its retail cost — which hit a new high this week and averaged $6.51 per gallon on Wednesday — is adding to voter anxieties about the cost of living ahead of November's midterm elections.

A timeline for the government's economic analysis was not immediately available. But the study, described by people familiar with the matter, is expected to forecast a mix of potential consequences — including both lower and higher prices — that could be used by administration officials either to justify or ward off a ban.

The study shouldn't be viewed as an indication the administration is leaning one way or the other, one of the people said. Instead, it's a standard analysis, like others routinely used by the White House to examine potential economic policies, the person said.

Energy experts have said export curbs could yield temporary price discounts on diesel initially, with refiners blocked from selling to foreign buyers. However, those short-term price reductions would likely fade swiftly — and be replaced with even higher costs — as rising US fuel inventories prompt oil producers and refiners to cut output.

articles.title: Trump FDA pick dodges vaccine, abortion questions at Senate confirmation hearing
articles.summary: Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), walked a fine line Thursday on vaccines and abortion, largely dodging difficult questions from senators. The confirmation hearing in the Senate Health, Education Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee shed light on the priorities of lawmakers, but offered little about Overton’s views…
articles.body:
Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), walked a fine line Thursday on vaccines and abortion, largely dodging difficult questions from senators.

The confirmation hearing in the Senate Health, Education Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee shed light on the priorities of lawmakers, but offered little about Overton’s views and how she would run the sprawling agency responsible for drug, tobacco and vaccine regulation, as well as the safety of much of the food supply.

Overton voiced support for established vaccines, seemingly contradicting Trump, who called the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine “lethal.”

“Every vaccine on the market right now are safe and effective,” including the MMR vaccine, Overton said, under questioning from HELP Committee chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.).

The MMR vaccine is the best public health tool to respond to the ongoing measles outbreak, she said.

Cassidy, a physician, has said Overton would need to repudiate Trump’s comments to secure his vote. But she wouldn’t directly answer whether Trump was wrong, and declined to say if she would stand up to the president or Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The Louisiana Republican has repeatedly tried to extract promises from administration health nominees to uphold scientific standards and not upend vaccine policy, to little avail. He was the deciding vote that allowed Kennedy to become HHS secretary.

“The secretary gave me guarantees. He later backtracked on those. He said he had to because the president told him to do something different,” Cassidy said. “If the President asks you to do something that goes against those guarantees you give us today, what will you do?”

Overton said she would “follow the statutory requirements” for FDA commissioners and give Trump her best advice.

Cassidy hasn’t said whether he plans to vote to confirm Overton, but he has voted for every other HHS nominee that came up for a vote in his committee despite his concerns. Overton needs the support of every Republican on the panel if every Democrat opposes her.

Overton is a top domestic policy adviser at the White House and a former chief policy adviser at a conservative think tank. She worked on a variety of administration health initiatives, including an executive order to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines.

Overton called that order “historic” and stood beside Trump in the Oval Office when he falsely claimed that the combined MMR shot could be “quite lethal.”

Later in the hearing, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) pressed Overton on Trump’s comments that Tylenol can cause autism if taken by pregnant women.

“I haven’t seen any casual evidence that Tylenol causes autism,” Overton said, but she wouldn’t say Trump was wrong when he told pregnant women not to take it.

“I’m really concerned that if an FDA commissioner will not tell the American public that the president is wrong about something, that poses a real threat to our health,” Hassan said.

“Dr. Heidi has been a ROCKSTAR in my Administration, where she has worked directly with Secretary Kennedy, Dr. Oz, and team, to deliver on the MOST TRANSFORMATIVE Health Agenda in History,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last month.

If confirmed, she would take over an agency roiled by an exodus of top staff and viewed by many in the healthcare industry as less trustworthy and more politicized than it has been in any previous administration.

She will have to navigate many of the same headwinds — political interference, funding cuts and balancing the demands of the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) movement with the MAGA White House — that plagued her predecessor, Marty Makary.

Overton would also inherit controversial initiatives such as a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone, and new FDA rules that make it easier for companies to put flavored electronic cigarettes on the market, even without approval.

Lawmakers pressed Overton on both issues.

Despite questions from numerous Democrats, Overton wouldn’t say directly whether she believes mifepristone is safe.

Overton is openly anti-abortion. She described the 2022 Supreme Court ruling overturning Roe v. Wade as “a huge victory for life.”

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) brought up a policy paper Overton wrote in 2023 while working at the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute, in which she argued “chemical abortions pose serious risks to women” and warned against allowing “abortion on demand” through telehealth prescribing of mifepristone.

Overton told Murray that mifepristone “has met the safety and efficacy determinations of the FDA.” Overton said she didn’t want to “prejudge” the FDA’s ongoing safety review of the pill, which abortion rights advocates condemn as politically driven.

They fear the results of the review could be used to further restrict access to abortions. Initial results are expected to be announced within weeks.

Overton’s views on mifepristone could complicate support among moderate Republicans.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who supports abortion rights, expressed concern that the mifepristone review is being driven by political pressure.

“This is a drug that is FDA approved, has been in use for well over two decades now,” Murkowski said. She said her state would be in a “very challenging position” if in-person requirements to dispense the medication are put back in place

But Murkowski said she didn’t want to ask Overton about it, because she didn’t expect anything other than “the exact same very specific technical responses” she had given other members who asked about mifepristone.

Overton will also likely need to win over the other moderate, pro-abortion Republican on the panel, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine).

Collins is facing a tough reelection campaign where abortion is one of the top issues of her race, and Democrats are seeking to undermine her reputation as one of the last Republican supporters of abortion rights.

But Collins focused her questions on flavored electronic cigarettes, and the administration’s effort to take down guardrails that have limited the tobacco industry’s growth in recent years.

Collins said she is worried recent approvals of fruit-flavored vaping products will jeopardize progress in reducing youth e-cigarette use.

Overton said the administration agrees about protecting kids from flavored vapes, but noted the recent approvals had the backing of FDA scientists, because the products helped adult smokers quit cigarettes.

articles.title: Microsoft puts Brad Smith in charge of communications
articles.summary: Microsoft’s communications are moving over to the legal and corporate side of the house.
articles.body: Microsoft is moving its communications group out of marketing and into its Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization. The surprise change will see Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith oversee communications, while the company searches for a replacement for Frank Shaw, chief communications officer, who is departing later this year. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella thanked Shaw “for everything he has done for Microsoft” in an internal memo announcing the communications changes. Shaw announced earlier this month that he’s leaving Microsoft after nearly three decades supporting the company’s communications. Brent Colburn, VP of global public affairs, has been appointed as interim communications leader to help navigate what Nadella calls “a media environment that is increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever.” Nadella also says he’s “excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story.” As GeekWire points out, that sounds a lot like how AI startups work, with researchers leading the demos and blogs at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft has been chasing Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI to “become one of the top four labs in the world,” according to Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. In an interview with The Verge earlier this year, Suleyman said he wants Microsoft “to build the very best frontier models in the world.” Brad Smith, who’s taking over communications from chief marketing officer Takeshi Numoto, is often the public face of Microsoft’s policy and corporate communications. Smith travels the world meeting with governments, regulators, and Microsoft’s customers. It’s still not clear who will take over permanently from Shaw later this year, but Microsoft is looking at both internal and external candidates. Here’s Satya Nadella’s memo: > Communications has never been more important to Microsoft. The company is changing, our industry is changing, and the world around us is changing. And in a media environment that is increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever, we need to continue to be grounded in our mission, earn trust each day, and find new ways to connect directly with all of our constituencies. > I first want to thank Frank for everything he has done for Microsoft. He has made tremendous contributions to the company and to our communications function over the last 17+ years. And he’s been a great source of counsel to our leadership team and to me personally, across the company’s biggest moments. > As Frank prepares to embark on his next chapter, Takeshi, Brad, and I have been discussing the evolution of comms at the company. I have asked Brad to lead the communications function going forward. Few leaders embody Microsoft’s voice as authentically as Brad. He brings a deep understanding of our business, a strong connection to our stakeholders, and a rare ability to communicate complex ideas with clarity, conviction, and trust. > During this transition, Brent Colburn will continue reporting to Brad and will now act as our interim communications leader. The comms leadership team will report to Brent, and Frank will continue to advise Brad and Brent on the transition. > In many ways, the people closest to the work have the best opportunity to shape how Microsoft is understood. We need to give people across the company the tools and support to do it well. And I’m excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story, all connected by a shared strategy and set of principles. All of you have a critical role to play in making that possible. > We have an exciting fall ahead, with a number of important moments and events coming up and great marketing behind them. It is a real opportunity to bring together our product story, our marketing, and our communications in new ways. > We will learn, we will experiment, and we will evolve. There is a fundamentally new way to think about communications, and this team will be central to building it. > Thank you for everything you do for Microsoft, and for the role you each play in telling our story. > Satya

articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter {beacon} Defense &National Security Defense &National Security The Big Story GOP lawmakers concerned after F-35 equipment ended up in China Republican lawmakers are concerned and are demanding more information from the Pentagon after sensitive F-35 parts were inexplicably diverted to Hong Kong and are now in…
articles.body:
GOP lawmakers concerned after F-35 equipment ended up in China

Republican lawmakers are concerned and are demanding more information from the Pentagon after sensitive F-35 parts were inexplicably diverted to Hong Kong and are now in the possession of the Chinese government.

Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC), told reporters Thursday that she is “very concerned” about China having possession of F-35 Lightning II components after they were diverted to Hong Kong this summer after being sent from Australia.

Fischer said she will ask the Pentagon for updates as the investigation unfolds and a briefing once the department has information to share .

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), another SASC member and China hawk, said he is concerned as well.

“China is not going to be our friend ,” Scott told reporters.

articles.body:
White House border czar Tom Homan stood behind Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Thursday, saying the agency is “not going anywhere” despite recent scrutiny surrounding its escalated enforcement operations.

“You can hate us all you want. We’re not going anywhere,” Homan said during an introductory speech at Department of Justice (DOJ) Victims of Violent Crime Summit.

Homans comments come as several use of force cases involving ICE agents draw lawmakers’ attention, and the agency breaks detention and deportation records.

On Sunday, an ICE officer in Austin shot Venezuelan national, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, while he was in his vehicle completing a food delivery for DoorDash. He was taken to the hospital before being released into ICE’s custody.

The Department of Homeland Security claimed the 28-year-old man “illegally entered” the U.S. under the Biden administration, which his lawyer has denied, and “had a final order of removal” from an immigration judge.

The shooting sparked backlash from Texas officials, including Rep. Greg Casar (D), who pushed for ICE to leave the Lone Star State’s capital. On the day of the incident, Casar called for “full transparency” from the agency as Austin officials investigate the shooting — days before the Associated Press reported the agent involved was not wearing a body camera .

In Michigan, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) directed state police to investigate an ICE vehicle pursuit in Grand Rapids over the weekend, which resulted in a fatal collision. Mario David Coronado Juarez, an undocumented immigrant from Guatemala, was killed in a car crash after allegedly attempting to flee from an immigration agent’s traffic stop.

While Homan did not mention these widely covered ICE-involved incidents during his Thursday remarks, he attributed the “hate” against the agency to members of the media after asserting, “We’re going to keep pushing. We’re not going to apologize.”

“ICE will continue doing the job every day across this country, especially in sanctuary cities, where we’ll surge resources and flood the zone. We’re going to enforce the law without apology,” the border czar said. “You got my word on that.”

articles.body: Meta’s lawyers have argued that certain evidence should be withheld from public view on the grounds of attorney-client privilege in the ongoing lawsuits over alleged harm to teens’ safety and mental health. Lawyers suing the company said this week that the label has been applied far too broadly, while pointing to a recently unsealed document showing that the team behind launching Instagram’s Teen Accounts in 2024 put in an order for baseball caps that simply said “a/c priv.” [Image: The lawyers suing Meta argue the Project Nido (an internal name for the Teen Accounts team) swag is part of “culture of privilege abuse at Meta” aimed at keeping the research it’s conducted internally on teen harm out of the public eye, an issue that Mark Zuckerberg discussed after internal data on Instagram’s effects leaked in 2021. US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers already called some of Meta’s privilege redactions “entirely inappropriate” in an order last month. She pointed out one example where Meta’s lawyers tried to cast a discussion about a slide deck and whether or not to publish certain data as a discussion of attorney legal advice, deciding that based on testimony from the trial, their reticence about publishing was more of a business decision focused on preventing leaks. articles.standfirst: Primeiro turno será em 4 de outubro e, segundo turno, se houver, em 25 de outubro. Veja quem pode trabalhar nessas datas e quais são os direitos.
articles.summary: Primeiro turno será em 4 de outubro e, segundo turno, se houver, em 25 de outubro. Veja quem pode trabalhar nessas datas e quais são os direitos.
articles.body:
Título de eleitor — Foto: Foto: Agência Brasil/Divulgação

Mais de 150 milhões de brasileiros voltarão às urnas em outubro para escolher presidente da República, governadores, senadores, deputados federais, estaduais e distritais. O que muita gente não sabe é que o dia da votação é considerado feriado nacional .

A previsão está no artigo 380 do Código Eleitoral, que estabelece que "será feriado nacional o dia em que se realizarem eleições de data fixada pela Constituição Federal".

Isso significa que o primeiro turno das Eleições Gerais de 2026 , marcado para 4 de outubro , será feriado em todo o país.

Se houver segundo turno para a eleição presidencial ou para a escolha de governadores, uma nova votação será realizada em 25 de outubro . Nos locais onde ocorrer, a data também será considerada feriado eleitoral.

🔎 Mesmo nos feriados nacionais, nem todos os trabalhadores são dispensados. A legislação permite que atividades essenciais e outras categorias autorizadas continuem funcionando nessas datas.

A existência do feriado não significa que todas as atividades precisem parar. O próprio TSE entende que empresas, comércios e serviços podem funcionar no dia da eleição, desde que respeitem a legislação e garantam aos trabalhadores condições para exercer o direito ao voto.

"O empregado pode ser escalado para trabalhar, desde que sejam respeitadas as regras aplicáveis aos feriados e, principalmente, seja garantido o seu direito de votar", afirma Marcel Zangiácomo, sócio do escritório Galvão Villani, Navarro, Zangiácomo e Bardella Advogados.

Para ajudar quem estará trabalhando no dia da votação, o g1 responde s principais dúvidas sobre o tema.

O trabalhador pode ter que trabalhar no feriado?

Como fica o direito ao voto de quem estará trabalhando?

E se o local de trabalho ficar longe do local de votação?

O que fazer se a empresa dificultar a ida às urnas?

Sim. Embora o artigo 70 da CLT proíba o trabalho em feriados nacionais, a legislação prevê exceções para atividades consideradas essenciais, como indústria, comércio, transporte, comunicações, serviços funerários e segurança, entre outras.

Além disso, o empregador pode solicitar que o funcionário trabalhe durante o feriado quando houver previsão em convenção coletiva, acordo firmado entre empregadores e sindicatos.

Como se trata de um feriado nacional, o trabalho realizado nessa data deve seguir as regras previstas para esse tipo de situação.

"Em regra, o trabalho em feriado deve ser remunerado em dobro ou compensado com outro dia de folga. Também é importante verificar a convenção coletiva da categoria, que pode estabelecer condições específicas", diz Zangiácomo.

A legislação brasileira garante ao trabalhador o direito de se ausentar pelo tempo necessário para votar, sem sofrer qualquer prejuízo.

⚠️ O empregador não pode criar obstáculos ao deslocamento nem adotar medidas que dificultem o exercício desse direito. Isso inclui descontos salariais ou a exigência de compensar as horas utilizadas para comparecer à seção eleitoral.

Na prática, a empresa pode ajustar escalas, flexibilizar horários ou adotar outras medidas para garantir o direito de votar.

Nesses casos, o tempo necessário para o deslocamento também deve ser considerado. "A empresa deve garantir condições para que o empregado consiga votar. Se ele trabalha longe ou em outra cidade, o tempo necessário para o deslocamento deve ser levado em conta."

O entendimento do TSE é de que o empregador deve adotar medidas que permitam ao trabalhador chegar ao seu local de votação sem obstáculos.

O trabalhador deve reunir provas da situação , como mensagens, comunicados, e-mails e testemunhos.

"A empresa não pode impedir nem dificultar o voto. Se isso acontecer, o trabalhador deve registrar a situação e pode procurar a Justiça Eleitoral ou os órgãos trabalhistas competentes", afirma Zangiácomo.

Além de violar um direito fundamental, a conduta pode configurar crime eleitoral . O artigo 297 do Código Eleitoral prevê detenção de até seis meses e multa para quem impedir ou dificultar o exercício do voto.

Quem enfrentar dificuldades para votar ou sofrer pressão relacionada às eleições deve guardar provas sempre que possível, aponta o MPT.

Mensagens de WhatsApp, e-mails, vídeos, áudios, prints de conversas, documentos e testemunhos podem ajudar a comprovar os fatos.

As denúncias podem ser encaminhadas ao Ministério Público do Trabalho , ao Ministério Público Eleitoral (MPE) e aos canais de denúncia dos Tribunais Regionais do Trabalho .

O trabalhador também pode procurar o sindicato da categoria para receber orientação e apoio.

articles.title: Ali Ghodsi CEO of world's one of the fastest-growing software company, says that key to making Databricks grow is to make sure he is not stuck in rooms with ...
articles.summary: With a valuation of $190 billion, Databricks has become one of Silicon Valley’s fastest-growing software companies.
articles.body: With a valuation of $190 billion, Databricks has become one of Silicon Valley’s fastest-growing software companies. But CEO Ali Ghodsi says the secret to scaling the company isn’t more meetings — it’s fewer. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on the Long Strange Trip podcast, Ghodsi explained that compressing his calendar and avoiding back-to-back sessions helps him focus on the company’s biggest challenges. Ghodsi further added that he makes sure that the top talent at his company is not suck conference room all day. Ghodsi revealed that at 8 a.m. every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, he and his team meet to identify the “main thing” — the biggest bottleneck facing Databricks. “I want to unblock that big thing that I think is going to get us 10x,” he said. Beyond those sessions, he avoids filling his calendar with meetings, warning that endless back-to-back schedules leave him “a slave to my calendar” and distracted by “monkeys on my back.”Databricks CEO: ‘I try to compress the calendar’Speaking on a recent episode of the Long Strange Trip podcast, Ghodsi explained that his approach involves intentionally avoiding filling up his schedule, even though it inevitably ends up busy anyway. The goal, he said, is to preserve open blocks of time so he can keep returning to what he calls the company's "main thing" — the single biggest bottleneck standing in the way of major growth.To identify that priority, Ghodsi said he and his team meet every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 8 a.m. to pin down exactly what that blocking issue is and figure out how to work through it together, with the explicit goal of unblocking whatever he believes could drive 10x growth for the company.Why he avoids back-to-back meetingsBeyond those recurring sessions, Ghodsi said he actively resists letting his calendar fill up with additional meetings. He described days packed with back-to-back sessions from morning until evening as days where he's effectively lost control of his own schedule, spending his time working through everyone else's priorities rather than his own — a dynamic he bluntly likened to carrying "monkeys on his back."Part of a broader executive pushback on meeting cultureGhodsi's comments reflect a growing sentiment among top executives who argue that meeting-heavy calendars often get in the way of real progress, even as companies face constant pressure to move faster. The data backs up some of that frustration: a 2024 survey by Atlassian found that nearly three out of four meetings fail to effectively communicate information, and 77% of respondents said meetings tend to simply generate even more meetings.This skepticism isn't limited to leaders at younger companies like Databricks. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has been especially blunt about his disdain for unnecessary meetings, famously writing "Kill meetings" in his 2024 letter to shareholders. That said, Dimon has been careful to note that not every meeting is a waste of time — he simply expects the ones that do happen to be treated with real focus and preparation. Speaking at Fortune's 2025 Most Powerful Women summit, Dimon said he always comes to meetings having done the necessary pre-reading, and expects full attention in return, saying he has no patience for attendees nodding off, checking email, or getting distracted by notifications during a meeting, calling that kind of behavior simply disrespectful.Other executives have voiced similar preferences for leaner, more conversational meetings over slide-heavy presentations, favoring direct discussion over sitting through decks read aloud.You use AI every day.
